title: "Employee Attrition Case Study"
author: "Alex Salvo"
output: html_document
---
#Executive Summary 

Employee attrition presents a financial and operational challenge for Frito Lay. The objective of this analysis was to identify factors significantly associated with employee turnover, develop classification models to predict attrition, and evaluate potential replacement costs. The dataset contained 870 employees and 36 variables, with 140 employees (16.1%) leaving the company.
Exploratory data analysis identified overtime, job involvement, and monthly income as three key factors associated with attrition. Employees working overtime had an attrition rate of 31.8%, compared with 9.7% among those who did not. Employees with the lowest job involvement had an attrition rate of 46.8%, compared with 8.6% among those with the highest involvement. Additionally, employees who left earned an average monthly income of 4,765 dollars , compared with 6,702 dollars for those who stayed. Chi-square tests and a Welch two-sample t-test provided sufficient statistical evidence to suggest significant associations or differences in means for these variables (p < 0.001).
Two classification models, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) and Naive Bayes, were developed using eight predictors: OverTime, JobInvolvement, JobRole, StockOptionLevel, WorkLifeBalance, MonthlyIncome, YearsAtCompany, and Age. The data was divided into 70% training and 30% validation sets. On the validation data, KNN achieved 67.8% accuracy, 63.4% sensitivity, and 68.6% specificity. Naive Bayes performed better, achieving 77.8% accuracy, 73.2% sensitivity, and 78.6% specificity. Both models exceeded the target of 60% sensitivity and specificity, and Naive Bayes was selected as the preferred model.
Additional findings showed that job role, stock option level, age, and years at the company were also significantly related to attrition, while years since last promotion was not statistically significant (p = 0.898). Financial analysis estimated employee replacement costs between $28,589 and $228,709 per employee, based on an average annual salary of $57,177 among employees who left. Providing a $200 retention incentive to the 77 employees flagged by Naive Bayes in the validation set would cost $15,400, although the effectiveness of this intervention remains unknown.
Overall, the findings suggest that Frito Lay should focus on reviewing overtime demands, improving employee engagement, and evaluating compensation competitiveness. The Naive Bayes model provides a potential tool for identifying employees at risk of leaving and supporting more targeted retention decisions.

# Introduction

This report investigates employee attrition using exploratory data analysis, statistical tests, and two classification approaches: K-nearest neighbors (KNN) and Naive Bayes. The objective is to identify factors associated with employee attrition and evaluate predictive performance using accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity.


## Data Import and Initial Exploration

```{r analysis-1}
# CASE STUDY LAY

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

#Import Data
employees = read.csv('CaseStudy1-data.csv', header = TRUE)

#Explore the Data

names(employees)
str(employees)
summary(employees)

#Check for Missing Values
sum(is.na(employees))
```

## Statistical Tests

Chi-square tests assess associations between categorical characteristics and attrition. Two-sample t-tests compare the mean numerical characteristics of employees who leave and those who stay.

```{r analysis-3}
#Statistical Tests for Employee Attrition

#Chi-Square Tests for Categorical Variables

#Chi-Square Test for OverTime
OverTimeTable = table(employees$OverTime, employees$Attrition)
OverTimeTest = chisq.test(OverTimeTable)

OverTimeTable
OverTimeTest


#Chi-Square Test for JobInvolvement
JobInvolvementTable = table(employees$JobInvolvement,
                            employees$Attrition)
JobInvolvementTest = chisq.test(JobInvolvementTable)

JobInvolvementTable
JobInvolvementTest


#Chi-Square Test for JobRole
JobRoleTable = table(employees$JobRole, employees$Attrition)
JobRoleTest = chisq.test(JobRoleTable)

JobRoleTable
JobRoleTest


#Chi-Square Test for StockOptionLevel
StockOptionTable = table(employees$StockOptionLevel,
                         employees$Attrition)
StockOptionTest = chisq.test(StockOptionTable)

StockOptionTable
StockOptionTest


#Two-Sample T-Tests for Numerical Variables

#T-Test for MonthlyIncome
IncomeTest = t.test(MonthlyIncome ~ Attrition, data = employees)
IncomeTest


#T-Test for TotalWorkingYears
WorkingYearsTest = t.test(TotalWorkingYears ~ Attrition,
                          data = employees)
WorkingYearsTest


#T-Test for Age
AgeTest = t.test(Age ~ Attrition, data = employees)
AgeTest


#T-Test for YearsAtCompany
YearsTest = t.test(YearsAtCompany ~ Attrition, data = employees)
YearsTest
```

## Predictive Modeling: Preparation and Train/Validation Split

```{r analysis-4}
#--------------------------------------------------------

#MODELING 


library(class)
library(caret)

#Select Important Variables Based on EDA
ModelData = employees %>%
  select(Attrition, OverTime, JobInvolvement, JobRole,
         StockOptionLevel, WorkLifeBalance, MonthlyIncome,
         YearsAtCompany, Age)

#Convert Attrition and Categorical Predictors to Factors
ModelData$Attrition = factor(ModelData$Attrition,
                             levels = c("Yes", "No"))

ModelData$OverTime = factor(ModelData$OverTime)
ModelData$JobRole = factor(ModelData$JobRole)

#Check for Missing Values
sum(is.na(ModelData))

#Split Data into Training and Validation Sets
set.seed(1)

splitPerc = .7

trainIndices = sample(1:nrow(ModelData),
                      round(splitPerc * nrow(ModelData)))

train = ModelData[trainIndices, ]
test = ModelData[-trainIndices, ]

#Check Training and Validation Data
dim(train)
dim(test)

table(train$Attrition)
table(test$Attrition)

#Check Attrition Percentages
prop.table(table(train$Attrition)) * 100
prop.table(table(test$Attrition)) * 100
```

## KNN: Dummy Variables, Scaling and Choosing K

```{r analysis-5}
#Convert Categorical Variables for KNN

#Select Predictor Variables
trainPredictors = train %>%
  select(-Attrition)

testPredictors = test %>%
  select(-Attrition)

#Create Dummy Variables Using Training Data
DummyModel = dummyVars(~ ., data = trainPredictors,
                       fullRank = TRUE)

#Convert Training and Validation Data
trainX = predict(DummyModel, newdata = trainPredictors)
testX = predict(DummyModel, newdata = testPredictors)

#Check Converted Variables
head(trainX)
dim(trainX)
dim(testX)





#Standardize Variables for KNN

#Center and Scale Using Training Data
standardizeModel = preProcess(trainX,
                              method = c("center", "scale"))

trainStandardized = predict(standardizeModel, trainX)
testStandardized = predict(standardizeModel, testX)


#Compare Different K Values

#Create Data Frame for Results
accs = data.frame(Accuracy = numeric(30),
                  Sensitivity = numeric(30),
                  Specificity = numeric(30),
                  k = numeric(30))

#Test K Values from 1 to 30
set.seed(1)

for(i in 1:30) {
  
  classifications = knn.cv(
    train = trainStandardized,
    cl = train$Attrition,
    k = i
  )
  
  CM = confusionMatrix(classifications,
                       train$Attrition,
                       positive = "Yes")
  
  accs$Accuracy[i] = CM$overall["Accuracy"]
  accs$Sensitivity[i] = CM$byClass["Sensitivity"]
  accs$Specificity[i] = CM$byClass["Specificity"]
  accs$k[i] = i
}

#View Results
accs

#Plot Accuracy by K
plot(accs$k, accs$Accuracy,
     type = "l",
     xlab = "K",
     ylab = "Accuracy",
     main = "KNN Accuracy by K")

#Plot Sensitivity by K
plot(accs$k, accs$Sensitivity,
     type = "l",
     xlab = "K",
     ylab = "Sensitivity",
     main = "KNN Sensitivity by K")

#Plot Specificity by K
plot(accs$k, accs$Specificity,
     type = "l",
     xlab = "K",
     ylab = "Specificity",
     main = "KNN Specificity by K")
```

## KNN: ROC Curve and Classification Threshold

```{r analysis-6}
#Find KNN Classification Threshold Using ROC

library(pROC)

#Choose K Based on Previous Results
bestK = 3

#KNN Cross-Validation on Training Data
set.seed(1)

trainClassifications = knn.cv(
  train = trainStandardized,
  cl = train$Attrition,
  k = bestK,
  prob = TRUE
)

#Extract KNN Winning Class Probability
knn_winprob = attr(trainClassifications, "prob")

#Convert to Attrition Vote Proportion
p_pos_knn = ifelse(trainClassifications == "Yes",
                   knn_winprob, 1 - knn_winprob)

#ROC Curve for KNN
roc_knn = roc(response = train$Attrition,
              predictor = p_pos_knn,
              levels = c("No", "Yes"),
              direction = "<")

#View ROC and AUC
roc_knn
auc(roc_knn)

#Plot ROC Curve
plot(roc_knn, main = "KNN ROC Curve")


#Find Optimal Threshold Using Youden's J
bestThreshold = as.numeric(
  coords(roc_knn, x = "best",
         best.method = "youden",
         ret = "threshold")
)

bestThreshold

#Classify Training Employees Using Selected Threshold
trainPredictions = factor(
  ifelse(p_pos_knn >= bestThreshold, "Yes", "No"),
  levels = c("Yes", "No")
)

#Training Cross-Validation Confusion Matrix
CMTrain = confusionMatrix(trainPredictions,
                          train$Attrition,
                          positive = "Yes")

CMTrain
```

## KNN: Validation Results

The validation confusion matrix reports performance on held-out employees. Here, `Yes` is the positive class.

```{r analysis-7}
# Evaluate KNN on Validation Data

#Run KNN Using Selected K
set.seed(1)

classifications = knn(
  train = trainStandardized,
  test = testStandardized,
  cl = train$Attrition,
  k = bestK,
  prob = TRUE
)

#Extract KNN Winning Class Probability
knn_winprob = attr(classifications, "prob")

#Convert to Attrition Vote Proportion
p_pos_knn = ifelse(classifications == "Yes",
                   knn_winprob, 1 - knn_winprob)

#Apply Selected Threshold
KNNPredictions = factor(
  ifelse(p_pos_knn >= bestThreshold, "Yes", "No"),
  levels = c("Yes", "No")
)

#Validation Confusion Matrix
CMTest = confusionMatrix(KNNPredictions,
                         test$Attrition,
                         positive = "Yes")

CMTest

#Accuracy, Sensitivity and Specificity
CMTest$overall["Accuracy"]
CMTest$byClass["Sensitivity"]
CMTest$byClass["Specificity"]
```

## Naive Bayes: Model and ROC Analysis

```{r analysis-8}
# Build Naive Bayes Classification Model

library(e1071)

#Use Same Training and Validation Data as KNN
NBTrain = train
NBTest = test

#Build Naive Bayes Model
NBModel = naiveBayes(Attrition ~ ., data = NBTrain,
                     laplace = 1)

#View Model
NBModel


# Find Naive Bayes Classification Threshold Using ROC

#Training Predicted Probabilities
NBTrainProb = predict(NBModel, NBTrain, type = "raw")

#Probability of Attrition = Yes
p_pos_nb = NBTrainProb[, "Yes"]

#ROC Curve for Naive Bayes
roc_nb = roc(response = NBTrain$Attrition,
             predictor = p_pos_nb,
             levels = c("No", "Yes"),
             direction = "<")

#View ROC and AUC
roc_nb
auc(roc_nb)

#Plot ROC Curve
plot(roc_nb, main = "Naive Bayes ROC Curve")

#Find Optimal Threshold Using Youden's J
bestThresholdNB = as.numeric(
  coords(roc_nb, x = "best",
         best.method = "youden",
         ret = "threshold")
)

bestThresholdNB

#Classify Training Employees
NBTrainPredictions = factor(
  ifelse(p_pos_nb >= bestThresholdNB, "Yes", "No"),
  levels = c("Yes", "No")
)

#Training Confusion Matrix
CMTrainNB = confusionMatrix(NBTrainPredictions,
                            NBTrain$Attrition,
                            positive = "Yes")

CMTrainNB
```

## Naive Bayes: Repeated Cross-Validation

Repeated resampling provides an additional view of the variability in Naive Bayes performance within the training portion of the data.

```{r analysis-11}
#Naive Bayes Repeated Cross-Validation

set.seed(1)

iterations = 100
splitPerc = .7

#Store Results
masterAcc = matrix(nrow = iterations)
masterSens = matrix(nrow = iterations)
masterSpec = matrix(nrow = iterations)

#Repeat Training and Testing
for(j in 1:iterations)
{
  
  #Split Training Data
  trainIndicesNB = sample(1:nrow(NBTrain),
                          round(splitPerc * nrow(NBTrain)))
  
  trainCV = NBTrain[trainIndicesNB, ]
  testCV = NBTrain[-trainIndicesNB, ]
  
  #Build Naive Bayes Model
  modelCV = naiveBayes(Attrition ~ ., data = trainCV,
                       laplace = 1)
  
  #Predict Probabilities
  probabilitiesCV = predict(modelCV, testCV,
                            type = "raw")
  
  #Apply Threshold
  predictionsCV = factor(
    ifelse(probabilitiesCV[, "Yes"] >= thresholdNB,
           "Yes", "No"),
    levels = c("Yes", "No")
  )
  
  #Confusion Matrix
  CM = confusionMatrix(predictionsCV,
                       testCV$Attrition,
                       positive = "Yes")
  
  #Store Results
  masterAcc[j] = CM$overall["Accuracy"]
  masterSens[j] = CM$byClass["Sensitivity"]
  masterSpec[j] = CM$byClass["Specificity"]
}

#Average Results
MeanAcc = colMeans(masterAcc)
MeanSens = colMeans(masterSens)
MeanSpec = colMeans(masterSpec)

MeanAcc
MeanSens
MeanSpec
```
